Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
40-year-old with history of childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever presents with 2-day progressive wheeze and dyspnea after heavy dust exposure. No chest pain, fever, or dizziness. Most consistent with an allergen-triggered asthma exacerbation; differential includes isolated allergic bronchospasm and early viral bronchitis. Pulmonary embolism considered low likelihood.   
Plan (per telehealth):  
• Attend local GP clinic today for objective assessment (pulse oximetry, peak flow/spirometry as available, focused respiratory exam).  
• Obtain/commence OTC antihistamine en-route if possible.  
• GP to consider SABA use review and need for oral corticosteroid depending on objective findings.  
• Letter sent via app to GP summarizing consultation.  
• Safety-net: seek urgent care if breathing worsens, unable to speak in full sentences, develops chest pain, or experiences syncope.  
No additional concerns raised by patient.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Asthma exacerbation (High) – prior asthma, clear dust trigger, typical nocturnal wheeze.  
2. Acute allergic bronchospasm to dust mites (Moderate) – temporal link to allergen, history of hay fever; less persistent symptoms expected but possible overlap with asthma.  
3. Viral acute bronchitis (Low) – common cause of new wheeze; absence of infectious prodrome makes less likely.
